name: Jade Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I grow vegetables at Westmarsh, two hundred and fifty hectares of carrots, leeks, cabbages and cauliflowers, all going to one big packer who supplies a supermarket. In November we're cutting leeks and lifting carrots every day, rain or not. I'm up at five looking at the weather, the orders and the crew list on my laptop, then out in the field by half six with the harvest rigs. By the afternoon I'm on the phone to the packer arguing about specs, that's the size and shape rules the supermarket sets.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In season I've got about sixty people, mostly seasonal pickers, and Dorota runs the crew. She's been with me eleven years and she's the best person on this farm, me included. Year-round it's six of us, plus my husband Ben, who retired from the police and now drives a tractor badly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like solving it. Tuesday's rain, Wednesday's order, a broken harvester and three pickers off sick, and you still get the lorry loaded by four. What wears me out is the supermarket. They change the spec on a Thursday for a Monday delivery and we plough in a field of carrots that are a centimetre too short.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I've got one that forecasts yields field by field from drone photos and the weather, and I ask an assistant to sort the crew rota and draft emails to the packer. It saves me two hours a day, easily. Ben thinks I talk to my laptop more than to him, which is probably true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's useful, I'll keep using it. At the growers' meeting I'd be the one saying, if you're not using these tools yet, you're making life harder for yourself. Some of the older growers would roll their eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's what I'm already doing. My problem isn't technology, it's the supermarket's buying power and the labour. If AI stays a tool, those problems stay the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add a soil-mapping service, about four thousand a year, to cut fertiliser. I'd keep pushing the packer to give us longer contracts. And I'd do the usual: hire the crew in March, plant in April, start lifting in July.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if I'm honest. I like a bit of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the spec being changed. Tell me about the worst time.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago, the supermarket decided carrots had to be eighteen centimetres, not sixteen, for a new premium pack. We had six hectares of sixteen-centimetre carrots ready. We sold some for animal feed at a tenth of the price. Supermarket buyers already want the carrots straight and the price crooked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the older growers roll their eyes. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the men at the meeting, to be honest. There's a grower called Desmond who calls my yield forecast my crystal ball. Last year it was right to within four percent and his guess was off by twenty. He still calls it my crystal ball.

S0.say: I'd say AI is useful and I'll keep using it, and anyone not using these tools is making life harder for themselves. Some older growers would roll their eyes.
S0.think: Privately it's what I already do. My real problems are the supermarket's buying power and finding labour, and those stay the same.
S0.do: Adds a soil-mapping service for about four thousand a year to cut fertiliser and pushes the packer for longer contracts. Hires the crew in March as usual.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly bored, since she likes some change.
S0.quote: Supermarket buyers already want the carrots straight and the price crooked.
S0.fieldNote: Confident and quick, already using AI daily for real decisions. Her grievance is with supermarket power, which she describes vividly. The Desmond story shows she's used to being dismissed and doesn't let it bother her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is probably how it'll actually go, because farming always lags. I'd also say firms not hiring beginners is a problem everyone's ignoring. We already can't find young people to train as managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, slow suits me, I can stay ahead. The bit that bothers me is the packer. If they need fewer young people in their office, it's fewer people who understand farming at the other end of the phone. That's worse for me, not better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on a graduate trainee manager, which I've been putting off, about twenty-six thousand a year. I'd make sure they learn both sides, the field and the data. And I'd ask Dorota to train them on the crew, because that's the part you can't learn from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, slightly uneasy about the next generation of managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does it matter who's at the packer's end of the phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when I ring to say we've had frost and the cauliflowers are going to be late, I need a person who knows what frost does to a cauliflower. If it's a system or a junior who's never seen a field, they just see a missed delivery and a penalty. Good packers have people who've stood in mud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Twenty-six thousand for a trainee. Can the farm carry that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just about, in a decent year. We've got about three months' costs in reserve. It's a bet. But I'm fifty-eight, and somebody has to run this when I stop. Ben certainly won't.

S1.say: I'd say slow change is how farming will actually go. Firms not hiring beginners is a problem everyone is ignoring, and we already struggle to find young managers.
S1.think: Privately slow suits me because I can stay ahead. What bothers me is the packer hiring fewer young people, leaving fewer people who understand farming at the other end of the phone.
S1.do: Hires a graduate trainee manager for about twenty-six thousand a year to learn both the field and the data. Asks Dorota to train them on managing the crew.
S1.feel: Calm, slightly uneasy about the next generation of managers.
S1.quote: Good packers have people who've stood in mud.
S1.fieldNote: Even as an eager adopter, she values people with field experience at every point in the chain. She plans for succession by hiring, not by family. The trainee is a real bet from a modest reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough for office people, and the government should be practical about it, retraining and help, not a shouting match. I'd also say some of those new AI jobs could be in farming, and we should go after them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine, probably better off. If the packer's office is run by assistants, the orders might get faster and cleaner. But I'd also worry they'd use the same tools to squeeze our prices harder, because they'd know our costs better than we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get ahead of it. I'd build our own data on costs per hectare, field by field, so I can argue with the packer on numbers, not feelings. I'd talk to two other growers about selling together, so we've got more weight. And I'd keep the trainee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be busy and mostly fine, but watching for the squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned selling together with other growers. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a woman called Priya Shah who does salad crops twenty miles away, and a family business, the Okafors, who grow potatoes. Between us we'd be a decent chunk of what the packer buys. It's the only way small growers ever get anything. One voice, three farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Desmond join?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Desmond would rather lose money on his own than make money with me. But I'd ask him. You never know. If the packer started squeezing him with machines, he might come round.

S2.say: I'd say it will be rough for office people and the government should be practical with retraining and help. Some of the new AI jobs could be in farming, and we should go after them.
S2.think: Privately I'd probably be fine or better off with faster orders. My worry is the packer using the same tools to know our costs and squeeze our prices harder.
S2.do: Builds field-by-field cost data to argue with the packer on numbers. Talks to two other growers about selling together for more weight, and keeps the trainee.
S2.feel: Uneasy, busy and mostly fine, but watching for a price squeeze.
S2.quote: It's the only way small growers ever get anything. One voice, three farms.
S2.fieldNote: Her response to more powerful buyers is to organise, which is unusual for a centrist and shows how practical she is. She reads AI as a power question between packer and grower. Still largely confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say both sides have a point, and we need a deal that shares the gains without wrecking things. I'd say farming should be in that conversation, because we're the ones still doing physical work and feeding people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a good spell for us, at first. Physical jobs are untouched, food still has to be grown, and if lots of office workers lose their jobs, I might even find pickers more easily. But that's a horrible thing to say, isn't it? That I'd do better because people are desperate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably hire some local people who'd lost office jobs, for the season, and pay them properly. I'd keep pushing the growers' group. And I'd put some of the money into a robot harvester trial, because I don't believe physical jobs stay untouched forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit ashamed of how well it might go for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hire people who lost office jobs. Would they last in the field?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would, most wouldn't, honestly. Lifting leeks in November rain is not something you get used to in a week. Dorota would sort them out in a day: who'll stay, who won't. She'd be kind but very clear. I've seen her do it with students.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why trial a robot when you've just said physical jobs are safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've read enough to know robots are coming. In this picture they're just not here yet. If I wait until they are, I'm behind. Better to know what they can do, so I'm the one deciding, not the packer.

S3.say: I'd say both sides have a point and we need a deal that shares the gains without wrecking things. Farming should be in the conversation because we still feed people.
S3.think: Privately I'd likely do well at first, and might find pickers more easily from laid-off office workers. I'm uncomfortable that I'd benefit because people are desperate.
S3.do: Hires local people who lost office jobs for the season at proper pay, with Dorota sorting who'll last. Puts some profit into a robot harvester trial to be ahead before robots arrive.
S3.feel: Uneasy and a little ashamed of how well it might go for her.
S3.quote: I might even find pickers more easily. But that's a horrible thing to say, isn't it? That I'd do better because people are desperate.
S3.fieldNote: She says the uncomfortable thing out loud and then looks at it. Her robot trial shows she is already thinking one picture ahead. Dorota appears again as the person whose judgment she trusts most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be ready, and growers who don't adapt will go under. I'd also say the people who lose their jobs, the pickers, the seasonal crews, need real support, because they're the ones who'll pay for this. I'd want that said clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd buy the robots. If they can lift carrots and cut leeks reliably, the economics are simple: sixty pickers is about six hundred thousand a year in wages and housing. The supermarket will want robot-grown prices within two seasons. The bit I don't like thinking about is Dorota and the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lease two harvest robots in the first year, maybe a hundred and twenty thousand, and run them alongside the crew to see what they can really do. I'd keep Dorota and make her the person who runs the robot side, with training. I'd tell the crew honestly, in March, that next year will be smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for the farm, but for Dorota and the crew, who've been loyal for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the crew in March?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it straight, in the canteen, before anyone heard it from someone else. Next year we're trialling machines, and there'll be fewer places. I'd give everyone who's been here three seasons or more first pick of the jobs that remain. And I'd mean it, because they've earned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Dorota say when you offer her the robot job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, so I go from managing sixty people to managing two machines. And she'd be right, it's a smaller job, even if it pays the same. She might leave. That's the one that would really hurt.

S4.say: I'd say growers who don't adapt will go under, and the pickers and seasonal crews who lose their jobs need real support. I'd want that said clearly.
S4.think: Privately I'd buy the robots, because sixty pickers cost about six hundred thousand a year and the supermarket will want robot-grown prices within two seasons. I don't like thinking about Dorota and the crew.
S4.do: Leases two harvest robots for about a hundred and twenty thousand and runs them alongside the crew. Offers Dorota the job of running the robot side and tells the crew in March that next year will be smaller.
S4.feel: Anxious for Dorota and the crew, not for the farm.
S4.quote: She'd say, so I go from managing sixty people to managing two machines. And she'd be right, it's a smaller job, even if it pays the same.
S4.fieldNote: She is clear-eyed and decisive: she'd buy the robots and says why in numbers. Her anxiety is entirely about people, especially Dorota. She knows her offer to Dorota is a demotion dressed up as a promotion, and she says so.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robot one, because it's the one where I have to tell people they're done. I'll survive it, the farm will survive it. What would help is real support for seasonal workers who lose out, retraining that they'd actually use, and some way of stopping the supermarkets taking every saving the robots make.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the savings. If robots cut my costs by half a million, the supermarket will want that half a million within two years. The question isn't whether robots come, it's whether growers keep anything when they do.

headlineQuote: Supermarket buyers already want the carrots straight and the price crooked.
portrait: Jade Santos is fifty-eight and grows carrots, leeks and brassicas on two hundred and fifty hectares at Westmarsh for a packer that supplies a supermarket. She uses AI every day for yield forecasts and rotas, and she's a quick, practical centrist whose real fight is with supermarket buying power. She meets each picture by getting ahead of it, from building cost data to organising with other growers. In the robot picture she'd buy machines without hesitation, but her worry is all for her crew and especially Dorota, her crew leader of eleven years.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries her most, because she would have to tell her loyal crew there are fewer jobs.
whatWouldHelp: Real support and useful retraining for seasonal workers, and a way to stop supermarkets taking all the savings robots make.
